challenges.name: backpressure-quiz
challenges.title: Is the queue absorbing the burst, or hiding it?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the submission queue: the metrics of an unbounded queue during the mock exam, and the admission log of the bounded queue that replaced it.

questions.question:
Mock exam, unbounded submission queue, 400 grader slots, average grading time 4.5 s:

time      arrivals/s  graded/s  queue depth  POST /submissions p95
10:00:00         340        89            0  120 ms
10:01:00         340        89       15,060  170 ms
10:02:00         340        89       30,120  180 ms
10:03:00         120        89       31,980  150 ms

The requirement is p95 2 s for submit acceptance.

Statement: "Every submission was accepted well within 2 s, so the queue absorbed the burst and the submission path needs no limit on queue depth."
questions.explanation: False. Acceptance is fast because accepting only means writing to the queue; the work is not done. Arrivals exceed grading by 340 - 89 = 251 jobs per second, so the depth grows by about 15,000 a minute, and a job accepted at 10:02 waits behind 30,120 others: about 30,120 / 89 = 338 s, more than five minutes, before a grader even starts it. Learners see a spinner, press Run again, and add more jobs to the same backlog. A queue smooths short bursts; when arrivals stay above capacity it only turns overload into delay that nobody is told about. Bound the depth by the wait you are willing to promise (throughput x maximum wait), and answer 429 with Retry-After beyond it. The misconception is that the acceptance latency measures the health of an asynchronous path; measure queue depth and age as well.

questions.question:
The bounded queue that replaced it: limit 5,000 for exam submissions, practiceLimit 2,000 for practice runs, 400 workers. The average of the last 200 measured grading times is 4,500 ms. Admission log, two requests 3 ms apart:

10:01:12.401 depth=4100 offer sub_88123 priority=practice -> 429 Retry-After: 24
10:01:12.404 depth=4100 offer sub_88124 priority=exam     -> 202 depth=4101

Statement: "Both decisions follow the design: the practice run is shed first because depth is above its threshold, the exam submission is accepted without removing any job already in the queue, and 24 s is the time for the queue to drain below 2,000 at the measured grading rate."
questions.explanation: True. Practice runs have the lower threshold, so at depth 4,100 they are rejected while exam submissions are still accepted up to 5,000; nothing already accepted is dropped, which keeps the 202 a promise. The Retry-After is the estimated drain time to the practice threshold: excess = 4,100 - 2,000 + 1 = 2,101 jobs, at 4,500 ms each over 400 workers: 2,101 x 4,500 / 400,000 = 23.6 s, rounded up to 24. The misconception this tests is that priority means dropping low-priority jobs that were already accepted; shedding happens at the door, by giving each priority its own admission threshold, and the estimate uses measured grading times so it tracks reality during the burst.

challenges.name: bounded-submission-queue
challenges.title: A bounded submission queue that sheds practice runs first
challenges.description: On the mock exam the unbounded submission queue accepted every job in 180 ms and grew to 30,000 jobs, so the last learners waited more than five minutes for a result. Implement class SubmissionQueue(config) on a fake clock (milliseconds). config = { limit, practiceLimit, workers, defaultGradeMs, window } with 1 <= practiceLimit <= limit. offer(job, now): a job { id, priority } is invalid unless id is a non-empty string and priority is "exam" or "practice": return { status: 400 } and count it nowhere. depth = accepted jobs still waiting. The threshold is limit for exam submissions and practiceLimit for practice runs. depth < threshold: accept, return { status: 202, depth } (depth after adding it). Otherwise return { status: 429, retryAfterSec } with retryAfterSec = Math.ceil(excess * sumMs / (count * workers * 1000)), where excess = depth - threshold + 1 and sumMs / count is the average grading time of the last `window` completed jobs (all priorities), or defaultGradeMs / 1 before any job has completed. Never drop or replace an accepted job. take(now): return the waiting exam job accepted first, else the practice job accepted first, else null; its wait is now minus its accept time. complete(jobId, now): the grading time of that job is now minus the time it was taken. depth() returns the waiting count. stats() returns, for exam and for practice: { accepted, rejected, started, maxWaitMs, avgWaitMs } where avgWaitMs is Math.round of the mean wait over started jobs (0 when none). Input: { config, jobs?: [{ id, priority, at, gradeMs }], burst?: { startMs, seconds, perSecond, examShare, seed } }. The runner simulates config.workers graders: at each instant finished workers call complete, idle workers call take, then each arrival is offered followed by take for idle workers; it runs until nothing is waiting or running and prints your stats plus invalid, maxDepth, depthAtEnd, lost (accepted but never taken), duplicateTakes, unknownTakes, lastFinishMs, a Retry-After histogram per priority and the first 20 rejections.
hints: Admission and dispatch are two separate decisions. Which one does the priority change at the door (when may a job get in?) and which one does it change at the worker (which waiting job goes first?), and what must never happen to a job that already got a 202?

Look at what each method needs to remember: one waiting list per priority in accept order (with the accept time), the take time of each running job so complete() can measure it, a list of at most `window` recent grading times for the estimate, and running totals per priority for stats(). The 429 branch uses the threshold of the job's own priority twice: to decide, and to compute the excess.

A worked trace with different numbers: limit 3, practiceLimit 1, 1 worker, defaultGradeMs 2000. At t=0 exam A arrives and is taken at once (depth 0). Practice P arrives: depth 0 < 1, accepted (depth 1). Practice Q arrives: depth 1, excess 1, Retry-After = ceil(1 x 2000 / 1000) = 2. Exam B and exam C are accepted (depth 2, then 3); exam D gets excess 3 - 3 + 1 = 1 -> 2 s. When A finishes at t=5000, the worker takes B (exam first, although P waited longer), and the next estimate uses 5000 ms instead of the default.

tests.name: Two workers, limit 4: practice runs are shed at depth 2, exam submissions at depth 4
Exam submissions are graded before older practice runs; waits are reported per priority
Retry-After uses the average of the last `window` measured grading times, not the default
A full queue rejects the new exam submission instead of dropping an accepted practice run
Excess counts only the jobs above each threshold, so practice waits longer than exam
Invalid jobs get 400 and are not counted; valid jobs around them are unaffected
Large: exam-day burst of 340 submissions/s for 60 s against 400 grader slots
Large: unplanned burst of 60/s for 30 s on the 40 always-on slots, with steady practice traffic
